title: The order of else-if tests
summary: Why a broad `if` test can take a result before a more specific `else if` test gets a chance.
objectives: Explain why an `else if` test is skipped after an earlier test is true.
Trace which grade a sequence of `if` and `else if` tests gives.
Put more specific score tests before broader score tests.
Recognize the same ordering mistake in other conditions.

blocks.text: Code Coach flags this pattern. The first test is broad: every score of 50 or more passes it, including 92.

bad.title: Code Coach's flagged pattern

good.title: Test the highest scores first

blocks.note: In an `if` and `else if` chain, Java runs the body for the first true test, then skips the rest of the chain. In the flagged pattern, `score >= 50` is already true for 92, so the later tests are skipped. This is a run-time logic mistake, not a compile-time error. Java accepts these tests and does not warn that the later tests will be skipped for this score.

blocks.text: An `else if` is checked only when every earlier test in the chain was false. So the order controls which test gets the first chance to match. In the flagged pattern, `score >= 50` includes all the scores that would also pass `score >= 75` or `score >= 90`.

blocks.caption: For a score of 92, the first true test wins

blocks.title: Think about overlap
blocks.text: Before writing an `else if` chain, ask whether a value could pass two tests. If it could, put the test you want to win first.
Follow the tests in order for `score = 92`. Stop tracing the tests as soon as one is true. That is what the program does.

blocks.caption: Tracing the flagged chain with `score = 92`
rows: Skipped because the first test was true
Skipped because the first test was true

blocks.text: The problem is not that `92 >= 90` is false. It is true, but Java never checks it in this run. Reordering the tests lets the score of 92 reach the `A` test first.
These complete programs show the run-time result. Each one compiles with Java 17. The broken version runs without a compiler error, but gives the wrong grade.

bad.title: Example 1: the flagged order gives the wrong grade

good.title: Example 1 fixed: the highest threshold comes first

blocks.note: With the flagged order, the first test passes and sets `grade` to `"C"`. With the fixed order, `score >= 90` is true first, so the program prints `A`.

bad.title: Example 2: a score of 78 is also caught too early

good.title: Example 2 fixed: 78 reaches the B test

blocks.note: The first test in the flagged pattern catches 78 too. In the fixed order, `78 >= 90` is false, so Java checks `78 >= 75`, which is true.

sections.title: See how the order changes results

blocks.text: Here are the grades for four sample scores. The chart counts how many scores get each grade. In the flagged order, all three passing scores get `C`; in the fixed order, they are separated into `C`, `B` and `A`.

blocks.title: A quick way to choose the order
items: Write down what each test means. `score >= 50` means 50 or more.
Check whether a value can pass more than one test. A score of 92 passes all three tests in the flagged pattern.
Put the narrowest or highest-threshold test first, then the next one, then the broadest test.
Trace a value that could match several tests and confirm it gets the intended result.

blocks.text: The same ordering mistake can happen whenever one test includes the values meant for a later test. These short examples show the pattern in other conditions.

bad.title: A broad age test takes the value first

good.title: Check the more specific age range first

blocks.note: Anyone aged 65 or older also passes `age >= 18`. The broad test takes the value first in the bad order.

bad.title: A large number is caught by the small-number test

blocks.note: Every number greater than 100 is also greater than 0. The same broad-first order hides the more specific result.

blocks.question: In the flagged pattern, what does the program assign when `score` is 92?
blocks.explanation: The first test, `score >= 50`, is true for 92. Java assigns `"C"` and skips the later tests. This is a run-time logic mistake; the chain itself compiles.

blocks.question: Which test should come first if scores of 90 or more should get `"A"`?
blocks.explanation: Put the highest threshold first. Then a score of 92 passes `score >= 90` before any broader test can take it.

blocks.question: In the corrected order, which test is checked next for a score of 78?
options: All tests are checked even after one is true
blocks.explanation: `78 >= 90` is false, so Java checks the next test, `78 >= 75`. That test is true, so Java assigns `"B"` and skips the remaining test.

items: An `else if` test is checked only if all earlier tests in the chain were false.
In the flagged pattern, `score >= 50` catches 92 before `score >= 75` or `score >= 90` can be checked.
Java accepts this ordering. The wrong grade appears when the program runs; the compiler does not reject the logic.
Put the most specific test first, then broader tests.
Trace a value that could pass several tests to check that the intended branch wins.
